guide_sections.heading: Compare index forms on one vector
guide_sections.body:
Each row below applies a different index to `x <- c(A = 10, B = 20, C = 30)`. The results come from the same three values, so differences in the output come only from the index.

```text
index                  values    names
x[c(3, 1, 1)]          30 10 10  C A A
x[-2]                  10 30     A C
x[c("A", "C")]         10 30     A C
x[c(TRUE, NA, FALSE)]  10 NA     A <NA>
x[integer(0)]          none      none
x[4]                   NA        <NA>
```

Rows two and three agree here, but they ask different questions: the negative index drops a position, while the names request labels in the order given, so `x[c("C", "A")]` would reverse them. The last row is the reason to validate positions and names before using them. Asking for a fourth element of a three-element vector does not stop the script; it returns NA with a missing name, which can flow into later arithmetic unnoticed.

exercises.approach: Read the index vector from left to right; each entry names one position to copy into the result.
exercises.why: In c(4, 8), position 2 holds 8 and position 1 holds 4. The index asks for 2, 2, 1, so the output is 8, 8, 4, and its length equals the index length of three.
exercises.wrong: Expecting a set-like answer such as 8, 4 with the repeat removed, or a sorted 4, 8. Indexing never deduplicates or reorders on its own.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `identical(c(4, 8)[c(2, 2, 1)], c(8, 8, 4))`, and `length()` of the result returns 3.

exercises.approach: Use a negative position: `c(2, 4, 6)[-2]` excludes the second entry and keeps the rest in order.
exercises.why: Position 2 holds 4, so the remaining values are 2 and 6. Exclusion by position does not depend on what the values are.
exercises.wrong: Filtering by value with `x[x != 4]` happens to work here but would drop every 4 if the value repeated. Writing `x[-4]`, confusing the value with a position, is worse: an out-of-range negative index is ignored, so all three values come back with no error.

exercises.approach: Validate first, then assign: check `!anyDuplicated(names(x))` and `key %in% names(x)`, and only then run `x[key] <- 9`.
exercises.why: The names A and B are unique and B is present, so exactly one entry is replaced and the vector keeps its length of two.
exercises.wrong: Skipping the checks. A typo such as "b" appends a third element, as Example 3 shows. With duplicated names, `x["B"] <- 9` would change only the first match and leave the second B untouched.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `identical(unname(x), c(1, 9))`; `length(x)` returns 2 after the update.

exercises.approach: Pick one indexing policy. To keep the first and third entries use `c(1, 3)`; to drop the second use `-2`.
exercises.why: Positive positions retain and negative positions exclude, so `c(1, -2)` asks two incompatible questions at once. R stops with the message that only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts.
exercises.wrong: Assuming R will keep position 1 and drop position 2, or wrapping the call in `try()` and carrying on with whatever came back. The mixed index never produces a value.
exercises.verify: The reference's tryCatch returns TRUE for the mixed index, and both `c(2, 4, 6)[c(1, 3)]` and `c(2, 4, 6)[-2]` return 2 and 6.

exercises.approach: Index the vector with `integer(0)` and inspect the length and printed form of the result.
exercises.why: No positions are requested, so nothing is copied. The result keeps the type and, for the named x in the reference, the names attribute, but has no elements.
exercises.wrong: Expecting NA or the full vector. Contrast `x[NA]`: a logical NA is recycled across every position, so it returns NA for each element instead of nothing.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `length(x[integer(0)]) == 0L`, and `print()` shows `named numeric(0)`.

exercises.approach: Before any keyed lookup or update, test names for duplicates and for missing requested keys.
exercises.why: R accepts `c(A = 1, A = 2)`, and `["A"]` returns only the first match, 1. A lookup by name therefore silently ignores the second record, which a real key column would never allow.
exercises.wrong: Treating names like a primary key in a table. Nothing enforces uniqueness, and a missing name returns NA rather than an error.
exercises.verify: `anyDuplicated(c("A", "A"))` returns 2, the position of the first repeat, so the reference check `> 0L` is TRUE.

run_note: The starter names three values A, B and C and supplies a mask of TRUE, NA and FALSE, then prints the named vector. Run it and read the names above the values. Predict what `x[mask]` returns before you try it: the NA position yields an unknown element rather than being skipped, which is why this chapter insists on known-only masks.
checks_note: The checks confirm that repeated positions duplicate elements, that a negative index drops only the second value, that a key is unique and present before it is updated, that an update by name changes only the selected value, that the guarded failure case really raised an error, that an empty integer index returns nothing, and that `anyDuplicated()` flags repeated names. They do not cover vectors whose names are missing entirely.
